b: As is customary when the world title is at stake, chess has found its way into the sports and culture sections of major international publications. The encounter between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov offers journalists a number of interesting angles, not least the contrasting trajectories of the two young grandmasters over the past twelve months.

Sunday's press conference and opening ceremony provided an opportunity for journalists to hear from both contenders. Gukesh's determination to approach the match as an opportunity to win the title anew, rather than as a title defence, was picked up by several publications. Meanwhile, the Uzbek media highlighted Sindarov's measured assessment of his chances.

Much of the coverage in the run-up to the match has revolved around the question of how relevant recent form will prove to be in a head-to-head contest. Sindarov's remarkable progress and Gukesh's difficulties since becoming world champion have prompted several observers to favour the challenger. The Indian grandmaster's previous experience of a World Championship match, however, is by no means an insignificant factor.

There is also plenty of reading material for those interested in aspects of the match other than the sporting contest itself. Bryan Armen Graham interviewed Sindarov for The Guardian, exploring, among other things, the Uzbek's competitive attitude towards his hobbies. Amit Kamath, writing for The Indian Express, took a closer look at the extraordinary collection of books surrounding the players at the Fondation Martin Bodmer.

From a rather different perspective, Canadian writer Stephen Marche uses the World Championship as a starting point for a reflection on artificial intelligence and the enduring appeal of human intellectual competition.
